planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early spring as soil becomes workable; Arisaema kiushianum is a compact Japanese species closely related to the more famous A. sikokianum.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; native to western Honshu and Kyushu in Japan, Arisaema kiushianum is a diminutive jack-in-the-pulpit prized by collectors for its dark purple, white-striped, pitcher-like spathe, which curls almost fully over itself so that light filters through the sides and front to reveal the inner striping. A slender tail-like spadix appendage extends outward beyond the spathe lip. Its small stature makes it well suited to a shaded rock garden or a prominent spot at the front of a woodland bed among other dwarf Arisaema relatives. As with all Arisaema, the tuber and foliage contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so site it away from pets and children.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; given generous moisture and fertile soil, Arisaema taiwanense is one of the larger species in the genus and benefits from a sheltered site protected from strong wind.

directions: Plant tubers in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial shade; native to middle elevations across Taiwan, Arisaema taiwanense is a large, architectural species that can reach 4-5 feet tall when grown with ample water and fertile soil. The mottled purple-brown false stem carries shiny, whorled leaves of 7-15 leaflets, each drawn out into a long, thread-like drip tip. The dark purple spathe, flecked with fine green dots outside and striped purple within, narrows to a dramatic filiform tail that can trail well over a foot beyond the hood. A choice specimen for collectors of large-growing Arisaema. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so keep away from pets and children.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade in early spring; Arisaema elephas is a high-elevation Himalayan and southwestern Chinese species that performs well in cooler woodland gardens with reliable summer moisture.

directions: Plant tubers in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; native to high-elevation meadows and mossy rocky slopes of the Himalaya and adjacent southwestern China, extending into Bhutan and Myanmar, Arisaema elephas takes its common name from its striking spadix, which emerges from the large green-and-mahogany-brown striped spathe as a dark, thickened appendage bent abruptly downward, resembling an elephant raising its trunk. The architectural divided leaves can reach several feet across on vigorous plants. Its origin at high altitude makes it one of the more cold-hardy Himalayan species for a shaded collector's border. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so keep away from pets and children.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early spring; Arisaema concinnum spreads gradually by stolons once established, slowly forming a colony in favorable woodland conditions.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; native to forest clearings and shrubby slopes from the Himalaya (Nepal, Sikkim, Bhutan, Assam) across to south-central China and northwestern Yunnan, Arisaema concinnum is a stoloniferous species that can reach 4-5 feet tall in good conditions. A single leaf divides radially into 7-13 narrow, pointed leaflets above a dark purple or green, white-striped, cobra-hooded spathe drawn out into a thin tail up to 6 inches long, appearing in early summer. Its spreading habit via stolons makes it useful for naturalizing in a larger woodland planting. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so site it away from pets and children.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade in early spring; Arisaema propinquum is native to high-elevation sites from Pakistan across the Himalaya to Tibet and is exceptionally cold-hardy.

directions: Plant tubers in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; native to high-elevation sites from Pakistan across the Himalaya to Tibet, Arisaema propinquum is a compact species growing to about a foot tall, with one or two large, trilobed, yellowish-green leaves. The dark purple, oblong-ovate spathe is prominently striped with white or purple and mottled toward the throat, narrowing to a short tail, while the spadix bears a long, thread-like appendage. Its high-altitude origin makes it one of the hardier Himalayan species, suited to a sheltered woodland or alpine-style shade bed. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so keep away from pets and children.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in early spring; Arisaema lobatum is a widespread Chinese woodland species, with some cultivated selections offering silver-speckled foliage.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; widespread across central and southern China in forests, thickets, and grassy slopes, Arisaema lobatum is a dioecious species producing one or two trifoliate leaves above a pale purplish or olive-green spathe boldly striped with purple, the funnel-shaped tube giving way to an acuminate limb drawn into a short tail. A pale green to whitish cylindrical spadix appendage sits within the hood. Easygoing and adaptable compared with some rarer Himalayan relatives, it is a good choice for gardeners building a varied Arisaema collection in a shaded woodland bed. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so keep away from pets and children.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)
